text: Why does a heavier external load usually reduce the shortening velocity of a muscle contraction?
options: Force and shortening velocity are constrained by the force-velocity relationship
Heavy loads remove all motor-unit recruitment
Velocity is unrelated to load
The muscle becomes longer because oxygen rises
explanation: As external load increases, the velocity at which a muscle can shorten generally decreases, although the relationship depends on contraction conditions.

text: Which statement about body mass index is most accurate for an elite strength athlete?
options: It measures muscle quality directly
It is a screening size index and should not be treated as a direct body-fat measurement
It identifies hydration status precisely
It replaces all body-composition methods
explanation: Body mass index is calculated from mass and height and cannot distinguish muscle, bone, water and fat compartments.

text: Which change is a common adaptation to appropriately dosed resistance training?
options: Abolition of the need for recovery
Permanent loss of all endurance capacity
Improved neuromuscular recruitment and force production
A guaranteed increase in every muscle's size
explanation: Resistance training can improve neural and muscular force-producing capacity, with adaptation depending on programme and individual factors.

text: Which adaptation can improve endurance performance after aerobic training?
options: Lowered capillary exchange
Reduced ability to use oxygen
Elimination of all anaerobic contribution
Increased mitochondrial and oxygen-transport capacity
explanation: Aerobic training can improve central and peripheral oxygen transport and utilisation, supporting sustained exercise.

text: The phosphocreatine system is particularly useful for which type of effort?
options: A brief, very high-power effort
Several hours of low-intensity exercise alone
Digestion after a meal
Long-term tissue remodelling without exercise
explanation: Phosphocreatine can rapidly resynthesise ATP and is important during brief maximal or near-maximal efforts.

text: An athlete sets a specific process goal for each rehabilitation session and reviews it afterwards. Which skill is being practised?
options: Randomisation
Self-regulation
External validity
Passive recovery only
explanation: Setting, monitoring and reviewing process goals are components of self-regulation and can support adherence.

text: After repeated high-intensity sessions on consecutive days, which nutrition priority is especially relevant?
options: Fluid restriction until the next session
Avoidance of all carbohydrate
Timely carbohydrate replacement alongside adequate total energy and protein
Replacing meals with a stimulant
explanation: Carbohydrate supports glycogen restoration, while adequate energy, protein and fluid support broader recovery.

text: Torque is the rotational equivalent of which linear concept?
options: Body composition
Temperature
Oxygen saturation
Force
explanation: Torque is a turning effect produced by force acting at a moment arm and is analogous to force in rotational analysis.

text: An athlete has good gym strength but struggles with repeated sport-speed actions. What should the team examine next?
options: Whether sport-specific speed, fatigue tolerance and decision demands have been progressively trained
Only the athlete's resting body mass
Whether all running should stop
Whether strength testing can replace sport exposure
explanation: Capacity is task-specific. Gym strength does not automatically demonstrate tolerance to repeated sport-speed, decision and fatigue demands.

text: Why can two athletes with similar tissue findings need different rehabilitation plans?
options: Tissue findings are never useful
Goals, beliefs, environment, support and sport demands can change the appropriate plan
Psychology determines all physical capacity
The calendar is the only meaningful variable
explanation: A biopsychosocial approach integrates biological findings with psychological, social, environmental and sport context.

text: A post-training change exceeds the smallest detectable change but not the smallest worthwhile change. What does that imply?
options: The test is invalid
The change is definitely important to performance
The change likely exceeds measurement noise, but its practical value may still be limited
The athlete did not change at all
explanation: Exceeding measurement error supports a real change, whereas practical importance requires a separate judgement.

text: Why should an athlete practise an unfamiliar testing movement before baseline data are collected?
options: It makes the test valid for every population
It guarantees a maximal score
It eliminates biological variability
Familiarisation can reduce learning effects that would otherwise resemble training change
explanation: Practice can reduce learning and technique effects, improving interpretability of subsequent baseline and follow-up results.

text: Inter-rater reliability asks whether which feature is consistent?
options: Different assessors obtain similar ratings or measurements
One athlete improves after training
A test predicts every injury
A sample contains no outliers
explanation: Inter-rater reliability concerns agreement or consistency between different assessors using the same procedure.

text: An athlete reports chest pain during a planned maximal test. What is the correct action?
options: Continue at a higher speed
Stop the test and arrange appropriate medical assessment
Ignore it if the athlete is highly trained
Average the result with the previous test
explanation: Potentially serious symptoms take priority over data collection; exercise testing should stop and the athlete should be assessed appropriately.

text: The area under a force-time curve represents which quantity?
options: Heart-rate variability
Body mass index
Impulse
Respiratory quotient
explanation: The area under a force-time curve is impulse, which represents the change in momentum produced by the force.

text: Why can acceleration counts from two wearable devices not be compared without checking their processing methods?
options: Processing never changes a signal
Acceleration has no relationship to movement
All devices use an identical calibration
Filtering, placement, sampling and proprietary algorithms may differ
explanation: Device characteristics and signal processing can change acceleration outputs, so methods and validity should be checked before comparison.

text: Which approach gives the most useful interpretation of a heart-rate variability trend?
options: Use consistent collection, examine the trend and combine it with sleep, illness, load and symptoms
Treat one low reading as a diagnosis
Change training for every small fluctuation
Ignore measurement conditions
explanation: Heart-rate variability is context-sensitive; consistent measurement and multi-source interpretation are more useful than isolated readings.

text: What is an important governance step before a team uses an artificial-intelligence model on athlete health data?
options: Upload identifiable data to any free website
Define purpose, access, consent, security, validation and accountability
Assume the algorithm is unbiased because it is numerical
Remove human review from high-risk decisions
explanation: Health-data technology requires a clear purpose, governance, privacy protection, validation and human accountability for decisions.

text: What does an effect size add to a p-value when reporting a training comparison?
options: The exact cause of the difference
Proof that the sample is representative
Information about the magnitude of the difference
A guarantee of clinical importance
explanation: Effect size describes magnitude, while a p-value addresses compatibility with a statistical model; practical importance still needs context.

text: A p-value below a pre-specified threshold does not by itself tell the analyst which fact?
options: Whether the sample produced an estimate
Whether the data were analysed
Whether a statistical model was used
Whether the effect is practically important or clinically useful
explanation: A p-value is not a measure of effect magnitude, clinical importance or probability that the hypothesis is true.

text: A highly specific test is most useful when a positive result is intended to do what?
options: Help rule in a condition because false positives are relatively uncommon
Rule out every condition after a negative result
Measure training load directly
Replace the clinical history
explanation: High specificity means few false positives, so a positive result can be useful for ruling in a condition when the test is appropriate.

text: Wellness data are missing mainly on days when athletes feel poorly. Why is this important?
options: Missing values always improve validity
Missingness may be systematic and bias the apparent recovery pattern
The missing days can be treated as normal automatically
No analysis is affected by missingness
explanation: When missingness relates to the outcome or exposure, complete-case summaries may be biased and the pattern should be examined.

text: The training principle of overload means that the athlete must receive what?
options: No recovery between sessions
The hardest possible session every day
A stimulus greater than the accustomed demand, progressed appropriately
A completely random programme
explanation: Overload provides a sufficient challenge to stimulate adaptation, but it must be appropriate, progressive and recoverable.

text: What is a reasonable expectation from low-intensity active recovery after a demanding session?
options: It should be maximal to be effective
It guarantees complete metabolic recovery
It replaces sleep and nutrition
It may improve perceived stiffness or readiness but does not erase excessive load
explanation: Low-intensity movement may help symptoms or perception for some athletes, but foundational recovery and training-dose correction remain important.

text: Which sleep intervention is most practical for an athlete with inconsistent bedtimes?
options: Build a consistent sleep-wake anchor and protect a suitable pre-sleep routine
Use a sedative without medical advice
Train later every night
Recover by sleeping only on weekends
explanation: Regular timing, a suitable environment and a consistent pre-sleep routine support sleep opportunity and recovery.

text: Why should repeated cold exposure not automatically be prescribed after every strength session?
options: Cold always causes injury
The purpose, timing, symptoms and possible effects on adaptation should be considered
Cold has no physiological effect
Athletes cannot tolerate any temperature change
explanation: Cold may alter symptoms and physiological responses; its use should match the goal and not be treated as a universal replacement for recovery planning.

text: Which combination best supports safe preparation for competition in hot, humid conditions?
options: Maximal training in the hottest part of the day for everyone
Extra clothing and no fluid breaks
Acclimatisation, cooling, work-rest planning and individual hydration
A fixed fluid volume regardless of sweat rate
explanation: Heat preparation combines acclimatisation, environmental planning, cooling, appropriate work-rest and individual hydration.

text: Which travel action is most useful immediately after arrival in a new time zone?
options: Ignore symptoms until competition
Stay awake continuously regardless of local time
Use alcohol as the primary circadian treatment
Anchor sleep and light exposure to local time while avoiding an immediate maximal load
explanation: A planned local sleep and light routine and gradual reintroduction of hard training help manage travel-related fatigue.

text: An athlete reports persistent low mood, withdrawal and loss of enjoyment. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Listen without judgement, assess safety and connect the athlete with appropriate support
Tell the athlete to train harder
Keep it secret from every professional
Diagnose a psychiatric disorder from one conversation
explanation: Mental-health concerns require respectful listening, attention to immediate safety and referral or support within professional competence.

text: What should a professional record after receiving a safeguarding disclosure?
options: A personal theory presented as fact
The person's words and relevant facts, actions taken and escalation through the correct pathway
A public team announcement
Nothing until the allegation is proven
explanation: Records should be factual, timely and secure, with appropriate action and escalation rather than speculation or public disclosure.

text: Which fact is important when considering a therapeutic use exemption?
options: A coach can approve a prohibited medicine
Any supplement can be authorised retrospectively
The treatment must meet the applicable medical criteria and the process must be followed
The athlete never needs medical documentation
explanation: A therapeutic use exemption requires the applicable criteria, clinical documentation and correct application or emergency process.

text: What is the main reason to adjust training during rapid growth or maturation?
options: Maturation eliminates the need for technique
Growth makes all strength work unsafe
Age alone determines exact load tolerance
Tissue tolerance, coordination, recovery and injury risk can change during development
explanation: Growth and maturation can change coordination, tissue stress, recovery and response, so training should be monitored and individualised.

text: Which responsibility belongs mainly to a host organising committee?
options: Delivering the operations of a particular edition of the Games
Writing the universal technical rules for every sport
Representing every national Olympic committee
Maintaining the global prohibited list
explanation: A host organising committee plans and delivers the specific Games edition, while broader Olympic and sport governance belongs to other bodies.

text: Which organisation is associated with governance of the Asian Games?
options: International Cricket Council
Olympic Council of Asia
Fédération Internationale de Football Association
World Anti-Doping Agency
explanation: The Olympic Council of Asia is the continental sports organisation associated with the Asian Games.

text: A National Sports Federation is primarily concerned with what?
options: Issuing all therapeutic use exemptions
Running every Olympic venue worldwide
Administration and development of its particular sport in India
Replacing the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports
explanation: A recognised National Sports Federation administers and develops its sport, including competition and athlete pathways within the national system.

text: Which function is consistent with the Sports Authority of India's athlete-support role?
options: Adjudicating all anti-doping appeals globally
Conducting all international sport-rule changes
Replacing every state association
Providing training, sports-science and support infrastructure through its programmes
explanation: Sports Authority of India supports sports development and high-performance preparation through training centres and athlete-support programmes.

text: Why must an athlete check the current Prohibited List rather than rely on an old list?
options: The list and sport rules can be updated, so current status must be checked
Old lists are always more complete
A medicine is safe if it was once permitted
Only coaches need to know the list
explanation: Prohibited substances and methods are governed by the current applicable list, so athletes and support personnel must use current information.

text: If emergency treatment requires a prohibited medicine, what should the medical team do after stabilising the athlete?
options: Hide the medicine from the record
Document the treatment and follow the applicable retroactive or emergency TUE process
Assume no anti-doping rule applies in emergencies
Ask the coach to approve the dose
explanation: Emergency care comes first, followed by documentation and the applicable therapeutic use exemption or notification process.

text: The World Athletics Championships are primarily a global championship in which sport family?
options: Only basketball
Only aquatic sports
Athletics and track-and-field events
Only cricket
explanation: The World Athletics Championships cover the international athletics programme, including track, field and related events.

text: A performance target conflicts with an athlete's immediate safety. Which principle should guide the decision?
options: The concern should be hidden from the team
The target always overrides clinical advice
The athlete must decide without information
Athlete welfare and safety take priority over selection or performance pressure
explanation: Ethical sport governance places safety, dignity and welfare at the centre of decisions, even when performance pressure is high.

text: Which pair contributes to external rotation of the shoulder?
options: Infraspinatus and teres minor
Subscapularis and pectoralis major
Biceps and brachialis
Pronator teres and flexor carpi ulnaris
explanation: Infraspinatus and teres minor are the principal rotator-cuff external rotators of the shoulder.

text: The plantar fascia is located on which aspect of the foot?
options: The dorsal hand
The plantar or sole surface
The lateral elbow
The anterior shoulder
explanation: The plantar fascia is a connective tissue structure on the sole of the foot that contributes to arch support.

text: During single-leg stance, the hip abductors help prevent which pelvic movement on the unsupported side?
options: Ankle plantar flexion
Elbow flexion
Contralateral pelvic drop
Thoracic rotation only
explanation: The stance-side hip abductors help control the pelvis and reduce contralateral pelvic drop during single-leg support.

text: The femoral nerve supplies the major muscles responsible for which action?
options: Shoulder external rotation
Finger abduction
Ankle eversion only
Knee extension
explanation: The femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps, the major knee extensors, and provides sensory branches to the anterior thigh and medial leg.

text: The anterior talofibular ligament is part of which ligament complex?
options: The lateral ankle ligament complex
The medial elbow complex
The cruciate ligament complex
The wrist extensor retinaculum
explanation: The anterior talofibular ligament is one of the principal lateral ankle ligaments commonly injured during inversion sprain.

text: Endurance training can increase stroke volume partly through improved ventricular filling and contractile function. What is the practical result?
options: No change in cardiac output
More blood ejected per beat at a given condition
Permanent resting tachycardia
Abolition of venous return
explanation: A larger stroke volume can contribute to cardiac output and cardiovascular efficiency during rest and exercise.

text: The respiratory exchange ratio is calculated from which two gas-exchange variables?
options: Sweat volume divided by session time
Heart rate divided by body mass
Carbon dioxide production divided by oxygen consumption
Blood pressure divided by stroke volume
explanation: Respiratory exchange ratio is VCO2 divided by VO2 and can provide information about substrate use and exercise intensity.

text: Which cardiovascular change may occur with heat acclimatisation?
options: Loss of sweating capacity
Complete elimination of skin blood flow
A permanent rise in core temperature
Expanded plasma volume and improved cardiovascular stability
explanation: Heat acclimatisation may expand plasma volume and improve cardiovascular and sweating responses, but does not remove heat risk.

text: A drop in force during repeated maximal contractions can reflect which broad phenomenon?
options: Neuromuscular fatigue
Improved motor-unit recruitment
Increased maximal oxygen uptake automatically
A normalised tendon reflex
explanation: A reduced ability to produce force after repeated effort is compatible with fatigue, although its central and peripheral contributors vary.

text: Oxygen consumption can remain elevated after strenuous exercise because the body is restoring several physiological systems. What is this commonly called?
options: Complete oxygen absence
Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption
The Ottawa rule
A limb symmetry index
explanation: Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption reflects elevated oxygen use during recovery processes after strenuous exercise.

text: Which parameter describes the number of electrical pulses delivered per second?
options: Electrode size only
Amplitude only
Frequency
Ramp duration only
explanation: Frequency is expressed in hertz and describes the number of pulses or cycles delivered per second.

text: Why is a coupling medium used during therapeutic ultrasound?
options: To prevent all heating
To cool the deep tissue automatically
To diagnose a fracture without imaging
To reduce air between the transducer and skin and improve energy transmission
explanation: Air reflects ultrasound energy, so a coupling medium helps transmit the ultrasound between the treatment head and the skin.

text: What should determine the dose of a thermal electrophysical agent?
options: Treatment goal, tissue, stage, safety factors and patient response
A fixed dose for every body region
The strongest possible sensation
The athlete's competition ranking
explanation: Dosage should be selected for the tissue and clinical goal while considering stage, contraindications, sensation and response.

text: A nerve-conduction study can provide information about what?
options: The exact athlete's motivation
The speed and characteristics of electrical conduction along a peripheral nerve
The amount of muscle glycogen
The quality of a training plan
explanation: Nerve-conduction testing evaluates electrical conduction characteristics and can help assess peripheral nerve dysfunction.

text: An isotonic exercise generally involves what?
options: Only passive movement by a therapist
No muscle activity
Muscle force with joint movement through a range
A cardiovascular measurement without movement
explanation: Isotonic exercise is commonly used to describe active muscle contraction with movement, including concentric and eccentric phases.

text: Which progression increases a squat's demand while preserving the closed-chain pattern?
options: Use passive knee movement only
Move immediately to maximal unstable jumping
Remove all lower-limb loading
Add appropriate load or range while maintaining alignment and control
explanation: Closed-chain exercises can be progressed through load, range, speed, surface or task complexity while preserving safe control.

text: Why might an athlete practise landing from a low height before a maximal drop jump?
options: It allows technique and load tolerance to progress before a larger demand
Low landings permanently prevent adaptation
A drop jump is always safer regardless of skill
It isolates cardiovascular endurance
explanation: Task progression should build movement quality and tissue tolerance before higher-impact or higher-speed demands are introduced.

text: A range-of-motion restriction is caused by pain and protective muscle activity. What should be addressed alongside mobility work?
options: Only longer passive stretching
The painful driver, strength, control and the functional task
The athlete's shoe colour
Nothing until the joint becomes completely loose
explanation: Mobility should be combined with management of pain, strength, control and task demands rather than treating range in isolation.

text: Which change is most likely to improve adherence to a home rehabilitation programme?
options: Use punishment for missed sessions
Give a long list without explanation
Agree on a clear, meaningful plan that fits the athlete's routine and monitor barriers
Avoid asking about goals
explanation: Adherence improves when the plan is understandable, relevant, feasible and collaboratively reviewed with barriers addressed.

text: The centre of mass is the point at which the body's mass can be considered concentrated for analysis. What happens when it moves outside the base of support?
options: All joints lock automatically
The body becomes weightless
The ground reaction force disappears
Balance becomes more difficult unless a corrective step or force occurs
explanation: Maintaining balance requires controlling the centre of mass relative to the base of support; corrective forces or a step may be needed when it approaches the boundary.

text: Why does the line of action of a ground reaction force matter at a joint?
options: Its distance and direction influence the external joint moment
It determines the athlete's blood type
It removes internal muscle force
It measures motivation directly
explanation: The direction and moment arm of an external force determine the torque it creates about a joint.

text: A movement in which the distal segment is free to move is generally called what?
options: A closed kinetic-chain movement
An open kinetic-chain movement
A passive-only movement
A respiratory cycle
explanation: In open kinetic-chain movement, the distal segment is relatively free; in closed-chain movement, it is fixed or weight-bearing.

text: Which variable is a kinematic measure rather than a kinetic measure?
options: Joint torque
Ground reaction force
Joint angle
Impulse
explanation: Kinematics describe motion such as position, velocity and angle; kinetics describe forces and torques that cause or influence motion.

text: Rate of force development is particularly relevant when the athlete must do what quickly?
options: Reduce all neural activity
Remain motionless for several hours
Measure body composition
Produce force in a short time window
explanation: Rate of force development describes how quickly force rises and is relevant to rapid actions such as sprinting, jumping and change of direction.

text: Which goal is most specific and measurable?
options: Complete three planned rehabilitation sessions this week
Get better soon
Try harder
Be confident sometime
explanation: A specific, measurable and time-bound process goal is easier to monitor than a vague intention.

text: Which combination may increase an athlete's perceived stress and affect recovery?
options: A stable routine and adequate recovery
Heavy training, poor sleep, selection uncertainty and travel
A completed easy session alone
A single normal hydration reading
explanation: Psychological, physical and environmental stressors can interact and influence sleep, recovery, readiness and performance.

text: What is the most useful communication style when an athlete is uncertain about rehabilitation?
options: Dismiss concerns to preserve authority
Use technical terms without checking comprehension
Listen, explain clearly, check understanding and involve the athlete in decisions
Give different instructions each day
explanation: Clear, respectful, two-way communication supports informed participation, adherence and shared decision-making.

text: Painful shoulder elevation should be interpreted with which additional information?
options: No information if imaging is available
Only one painful arc observation
Only the athlete's age
History, strength, range, cervical screen and functional pattern
explanation: Shoulder pain is multifactorial; examination should integrate history, movement, strength, cervical and neurological findings and function.

text: Pain above the ankle after external rotation and dorsiflexion trauma should raise consideration of what?
options: A syndesmotic injury
Only plantar fasciitis
A rotator-cuff tear
A cervical disc lesion
explanation: High-ankle or syndesmotic injury should be considered when the mechanism and pain location fit, with appropriate examination and imaging decisions.

text: Why can a cluster of compatible findings be more useful than one isolated special test?
options: Clusters guarantee a diagnosis
Several findings may change clinical probability more than one finding alone
One test is always invalid
Clusters remove the need for history
explanation: Combining history and compatible examination findings can improve diagnostic reasoning, although no cluster is infallible.

text: Which finding should lower the threshold for medical referral in a musculoskeletal presentation?
options: A stable painless squat
A familiar mild post-training ache
Unexplained constitutional symptoms, progressive neurological loss or severe non-mechanical pain
An expected response to a new exercise
explanation: Systemic features, progressive neurological deficit and severe non-mechanical pain can indicate serious pathology and require escalation.

text: What makes an outcome measure useful for follow-up?
options: It replaces patient goals
It always produces a higher score
It requires no standardised method
It is relevant, sufficiently reliable, responsive and interpretable for the decision
explanation: A useful outcome measure should capture a relevant construct with acceptable measurement properties and support interpretation over time.

text: What should happen if concussion symptoms increase during a graduated activity step?
options: Stop or reduce the progression and reassess before advancing
Double the next exercise dose
Ignore symptoms if balance is normal
Clear the athlete because symptoms are expected
explanation: Symptoms during progression require a pause or reduction and reassessment within the clinical return-to-sport plan.

text: Which factor is important before progressing an ACL-reconstruction athlete to demanding change-of-direction work?
options: Time since surgery alone
Adequate strength, movement quality, confidence and tolerance of graded loading
A normal seated range only
The athlete's selection status
explanation: ACL progression should be criteria-based and consider strength, movement, symptoms, psychological readiness and sport-specific exposure.

text: In an athlete with groin pain, why should the clinician examine more than the painful adductor?
options: The examination cannot change management
All groin pain comes from the adductor
Hip, abdominal, inguinal, pubic, lumbar and other causes may contribute to symptoms
A history is unnecessary
explanation: Groin pain has several clinically defined and non-musculoskeletal causes, so examination and differential diagnosis should be broad enough to be safe.

text: An athlete has neck pain and limb tingling after a collision. What is the safest immediate approach?
options: Ask the athlete to walk off alone
Force the neck through range to check stiffness
Return the athlete if strength seems normal
Stabilise, assess systematically and activate emergency medical care
explanation: Neck pain with neurological symptoms after trauma requires protection, systematic assessment and appropriate emergency escalation.

text: Why is a high acute workload not automatically an injury diagnosis?
options: Load interacts with capacity, recovery, prior exposure, symptoms and context
Load data are never useful
Every high load causes injury
Only pain-free athletes have risk
explanation: Training load is one part of a complex system; risk interpretation requires exposure history, capacity, recovery, symptoms and context.

text: Why may sodium replacement matter during prolonged exercise in heavy sweaters?
options: Sodium is never lost in sweat
Sodium losses and fluid needs vary, so a tailored plan may support fluid balance
A fixed high dose is safe for everyone
Sodium replaces carbohydrate energy
explanation: Sweat sodium losses vary between athletes and conditions; hydration and sodium plans should be individualised and avoid overdrinking.

text: A cohort study generally follows groups with different exposures to observe which outcome?
options: The exact mechanism in every individual
Only the immediate effect of randomisation
The incidence of an outcome over time
A laboratory force curve
explanation: Cohort studies observe outcomes over time in groups defined by exposure, but confounding can limit causal interpretation.

text: A rehabilitation study finds a statistically significant improvement smaller than the patient's meaningful change threshold. What should be reported?
options: Patient-reported outcomes should be discarded
The treatment is definitely useless
The p-value proves a large benefit
The result may be statistically detectable but not meaningful to the patient
explanation: Statistical detectability and patient or sport relevance are different; both should be reported and interpreted.

text: Which finding best supports a patellar-tendon load problem in this athlete?
options: Localised inferior-patellar pain reproduced by jumping and resisted knee extension
Pain only during wrist gripping
Numbness in the hand
Pain only with quiet sitting after travel
explanation: Patellar tendinopathy commonly produces load-related pain localised to the tendon, especially with jumping or knee-extensor demand.
passage: A volleyball player reports six weeks of pain at the inferior pole of the patella. Pain is worse after repeated jumps and is reproduced by a decline squat, but there is no locking, fever or traumatic swelling.

text: Which early intervention is most defensible?
options: Stop all knee loading permanently
Modify jump volume and introduce progressive tendon loading within a monitored response
Perform maximal jumping every day
Use passive treatment without exercise
explanation: Load modification and progressive strengthening address capacity while monitoring symptoms and next-day response.
passage: A volleyball player reports six weeks of pain at the inferior pole of the patella. Pain is worse after repeated jumps and is reproduced by a decline squat, but there is no locking, fever or traumatic swelling.

text: Which training variable should be monitored closely during the return to volleyball?
options: Only the number of stretching minutes
Only body mass
Jump frequency, intensity, surface, recovery and next-day symptoms
The athlete's preferred jersey
explanation: The relevant external load and internal response should be monitored as jumping exposure is progressed.
passage: A volleyball player reports six weeks of pain at the inferior pole of the patella. Pain is worse after repeated jumps and is reproduced by a decline squat, but there is no locking, fever or traumatic swelling.

text: Which criterion is most useful before a full match return?
options: A single passive knee test
A pain-free walk only
A fixed date irrespective of response
Progressive practice and match-like jumping tolerated without unacceptable symptoms or loss of function
explanation: Return should demonstrate tolerance of the sport's jumping demands with acceptable symptoms, function and recovery response.
passage: A volleyball player reports six weeks of pain at the inferior pole of the patella. Pain is worse after repeated jumps and is reproduced by a decline squat, but there is no locking, fever or traumatic swelling.

text: Which pattern is most consistent with rotator-cuff-related shoulder pain?
options: Pain with overhead loading and resisted elevation, interpreted with the full examination
Pain only during ankle hopping
Numbness isolated to the foot
A painless full-speed throw
explanation: Rotator-cuff-related pain often involves overhead or resisted shoulder loading, but diagnosis should not rely on one test alone.
passage: A baseball pitcher develops gradual lateral shoulder pain after a sudden increase in throwing volume. Strength is mildly painful but not absent, and there is no traumatic dislocation or neurological deficit.

text: What is the most appropriate early training modification?
options: Continue the full throwing schedule
Reduce provocative throwing volume while maintaining tolerable conditioning and progressive shoulder capacity
Stop all movement for the entire season
Test maximal velocity every day
explanation: Load should be modified to reduce aggravating exposure while strength, control and general conditioning are maintained and progressed.
passage: A baseball pitcher develops gradual lateral shoulder pain after a sudden increase in throwing volume. Strength is mildly painful but not absent, and there is no traumatic dislocation or neurological deficit.

text: Which feature would warrant a broader or more urgent assessment?
options: Mild fatigue after a normal session
Gradual pain that settles with reduced volume
Acute major weakness after trauma, deformity or progressive neurological symptoms
A normal painless cervical screen
explanation: Traumatic deformity, major weakness or progressive neurological findings can indicate significant injury and require appropriate escalation.
passage: A baseball pitcher develops gradual lateral shoulder pain after a sudden increase in throwing volume. Strength is mildly painful but not absent, and there is no traumatic dislocation or neurological deficit.

text: Which progression best restores the athlete's throwing demand?
options: Ignore the response because the season is short
Return immediately to full competitive pitching
Use passive range as the only criterion
Increase distance, volume, intensity and recovery demands in staged steps
explanation: Throwing progression should rebuild the relevant volume, intensity, distance and recovery demands while monitoring symptoms and control.
passage: A baseball pitcher develops gradual lateral shoulder pain after a sudden increase in throwing volume. Strength is mildly painful but not absent, and there is no traumatic dislocation or neurological deficit.

text: Which finding most supports nerve-root involvement rather than uncomplicated local back pain?
options: Radiating leg pain with neurological change in a consistent distribution
Pain only after local trunk fatigue
Normal strength, sensation and reflexes
A symptom that resolves with a warm-up
explanation: Radiating symptoms with corresponding neurological findings increase concern for nerve-root involvement and guide examination or referral.
passage: A gymnast reports low-back pain with new radiating pain to the lateral leg. Straight-leg raise reproduces familiar symptoms, and ankle dorsiflexion is weaker than on the other side.

text: Which assessment should be prioritised before routine strengthening?
options: Test maximal deadlift capacity
Document myotomes, sensation, reflexes, neural signs and red flags
Stretch the nerve repeatedly into symptoms
Clear the athlete because they can walk
explanation: Neurological deficits require systematic examination and monitoring before routine progression is chosen.
passage: A gymnast reports low-back pain with new radiating pain to the lateral leg. Straight-leg raise reproduces familiar symptoms, and ankle dorsiflexion is weaker than on the other side.

text: Which development would require urgent escalation?
options: Improvement with a graded walk
Mild stiffness after sitting
Progressive weakness, saddle sensory change or bladder disturbance
Stable symptoms with a normal neurological screen
explanation: Progressive neurological deficit, saddle sensory change and bladder disturbance are urgent red flags.
passage: A gymnast reports low-back pain with new radiating pain to the lateral leg. Straight-leg raise reproduces familiar symptoms, and ankle dorsiflexion is weaker than on the other side.

text: If urgent pathology is excluded and symptoms improve, what should later rehabilitation include?
options: Treatment based only on imaging appearance
Immediate maximal gymnastics under fatigue
Permanent avoidance of all spinal movement
Graded trunk, hip and sport-specific loading guided by neurological response
